Fake Nike Website Scam UK: Spot a Counterfeit Shop

Fake Nike websites are getting harder to spot—but there are telltale signs that separate the real shop from the scam.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-05-10 · Updated 2026-07-26 · 9 min read

fake nike website uknike scam websitecounterfeit nike trainers uk
Quick answer: SNKRS shows how Nike releases coveted shoes, but Nike also supplies authorised retailers and SNKRS can reserve pairs at nearby retailers. Treat an unfamiliar seller offering scarce shoes in every size far below normal prices as high risk, then verify the retailer independently. If you paid or received suspected counterfeits, preserve the listing, shoes, box and payment evidence.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

No single signal decides it — weigh several together

Trainer advice usually opens with the discount. The more useful opening is that no single fact about a sneaker listing settles the question, so the method has to be a risk screen rather than a test with one answer.

Availability that conflicts with how Nike released a shoe is genuinely useful evidence. It is not proof, because Nike does not sell only through its own app and site: it refers to Nike-authorised retailers, and stock also reaches resale sellers who acquired it lawfully. So collect several signals and read how they combine:

  • Seller identity, established away from the seller's own website and advertising.
  • Release history: does this exact shoe, in these sizes, square with how and when Nike released it?
  • Price, read against both retail and the current resale market rather than retail alone.
  • Payment method, and whether it leaves you any route back.
  • Returns and complaints information, and whether it names a company you can look up.
  • The domain, opened by typing it rather than by following a link.

One weak signal is a reason to look harder. Several at once — an unfamiliar seller, a scarce release, a full size run, a price far below the market and a payment method with no recourse — is the pattern to walk away from.

How Nike releases coveted shoes, and where else they legitimately appear

Nike describes SNKRS as its destination for highly coveted releases, and its help pages document a launch calendar, SNKRS Drawings and SNKRS Pass reservations. In a Drawing you enter inside a window and learn afterwards whether you were selected. A SNKRS Pass reserves a pair, and Nike's own SNKRS material says selected pairs may be reserved for collection at a nearby retailer, not only at a Nike store. SNKRS Reserve works differently again: it can make sizes to order during a limited pre-order window.

That is why the release mechanism is a lead rather than a conclusion. A shop holding stock of a sold-out shoe is not describing something impossible, so check the specific release in Nike's launch calendar and then check the specific seller. Do not accept a seller's own claim to be authorised: Nike lists its own stores in a retail directory, and an established sports retailer is something you can confirm away from its advertising. Allocation, date and provenance all still need checking on the individual listing.

Genuine resale is not the same thing as counterfeit

Paying more than retail for a sold-out pair is a normal, lawful transaction. Resale is an established market, scarcity genuinely pushes prices up, and a high asking price is not by itself a fraud signal.

The risk lives in the seller and the payment rather than in the figure. Above retail, from a seller whose authentication process you can examine, is a premium you are choosing to pay. Brand new, in every size, well under the market, from a site you had not heard of yesterday, is the combination worth refusing.

Scale and familiarity are not verification either. In 2024 Nike and Converse brought a US lawsuit against alleged counterfeiting networks; reporting on that case describes 52 alleged networks operating 98 websites and 267 social media handles. Separately, Nike has taken legal action against StockX. Neither of those is a judgement on any listing in front of you. They are only a reason not to treat a platform's size as a substitute for checking a seller.

Factory, outlet and clearance are not the test

Nike operates genuine Factory and Clearance stores and lists its UK stores in its own retail directory, so the word in a domain is not the finding. What matters is whether the address is exactly the one Nike publishes, and whether the company behind an unfamiliar one can be identified at all.

  • Type the address by hand. nike.com opened yourself is not the same thing as a lookalike reached from an advert.
  • Check any address you were sent against Nike's own help pages and store directory, which you get to from the address you typed, rather than against a search result.
  • Identify the company independently. A named, established sports retailer can be checked away from its own site; an anonymous shop cannot.
  • Prefer a payment route with recourse, because bank transfer, cryptocurrency and gift-card codes remove yours.
  • Read the returns and complaints information and ask whether a real business could operate on it.

What happens if counterfeit goods reach the UK border

GOV.UK sets out the process. Border Force can detain goods it suspects infringe intellectual property rights. Under the standard procedure, where the rights holder confirms the goods infringe and the importer or owner agrees or does not respond, the goods can be destroyed. An objection can instead lead to court proceedings or to the goods being released, so a rights holder's confirmation does not automatically close every case. Small postal or courier consignments can follow a separate simplified procedure.

The Government's customs intellectual property enforcement report covering 2021 to 2023 says destruction was the main outcome for articles confirmed as counterfeit.

For a shopper the practical reading is blunt: money paid overseas for counterfeit goods can end up buying nothing at all, with no seller left to argue with.

The unexpected customs fee

Do not pay through an unexpected customs link. Check the parcel directly with the courier using contact details you obtained independently. Genuine import VAT or duty may be collected by the parcel company, while confirmed counterfeit goods are handled through the Border Force infringement process rather than released because a shopper pays a surprise fee.

GOV.UK explains when VAT, customs duty and handling charges apply to goods sent from abroad, so a charge existing at all is not the tell. What marks out the scam version is the route it arrives by: an unexpected message, a short deadline, and a payment page you did not reach by going to the parcel company yourself.

If you already paid

Keep the shoes and the box if anything arrived, together with the order page, the advert and any tracking reference. Do not assume Nike will authenticate them for you — its public help material does not promise that its ordinary contact channels will inspect a suspected counterfeit. Report the seller through the contact route on nike.com, hold on to the physical evidence, and ask Citizens Advice or your card issuer what to do next.

On the money: a Section 75 claim under the Consumer Credit Act 1974 may be available on a credit-funded purchase. It depends on the required relationship between the credit and the supplier, and on a cash price — per item, or per qualifying set — of more than £100 and no more than £30,000. A £160 pair might therefore fall inside it where the identical pair bought on a debit card does not, but the figure and the card type do not settle a claim between them; MoneyHelper is the place to read what a covered arrangement looks like.

Debit purchases lean on chargeback, governed by each card scheme's own rules and deadlines rather than by statute. A bank transfer to a shop that has stopped replying needs a call to your bank immediately.

Citizens Advice sets out the refund position for counterfeit goods. That guidance is published as advice for England, with its own Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland versions, so use the one for your nation. Our scam recovery checklist puts these steps in order.

Reporting a fake Nike shop

One limitation worth stating plainly: several third-party sites publish Nike brand-protection email addresses that we could not match against Nike's own published contacts, so we do not repeat them here. Use the contact route on nike.com, reached by typing the address in yourself.

  • The web address itself goes to the NCSC, through its scam-website reporting form.
  • Phishing emails go to report@phishing.gov.uk.
  • A suspicious SMS text can be forwarded to 7726, free of charge.
  • Paid adverts are the Advertising Standards Authority's remit; the platform that ran one should hear about it as well.
  • Money lost goes into a Report Fraud report — reportfraud.police.uk, or 0300 123 2040. In Scotland: Police Scotland, on 101.
  • Counterfeit goods have a route of their own. The Citizens Advice consumer helpline, on 0808 223 1133, passes reports to Trading Standards.

Frequently asked questions

A site has a sold-out release in every size at half price. Is that possible?

It is a high-risk claim, especially after a scarce release has sold out, but it is not impossible by definition. Check the exact release in Nike's launch calendar, verify whether the seller is an established retailer, and do not rely on the seller's own claim that it is authorised.

Is paying above retail on a resale platform a scam?

Not in itself. Resale is a legitimate market and scarcity genuinely pushes prices up. The risk lives in the seller's authentication process and in your payment protection, not in the fact that the figure exceeds what Nike charged.

What is SNKRS, and does buying elsewhere mean a shop is fake?

SNKRS is Nike's destination for highly coveted releases, with a launch calendar, Drawings and Pass reservations, and SNKRS Reserve can make sizes to order in a limited pre-order window. It is not the only route. Nike refers to Nike-authorised retailers, and a SNKRS Pass can reserve selected pairs at a nearby retailer, so buying elsewhere proves nothing on its own.

Could customs really destroy trainers I have paid for?

Border Force can detain goods it suspects infringe intellectual property rights, and under the standard process they can be destroyed where the rights holder confirms infringement and the importer or owner agrees or does not respond. An objection can lead to proceedings or release instead. Government reporting covering 2021 to 2023 says destruction was the main outcome for articles confirmed as counterfeit.

A message says my parcel is held and a fee is due. Is that always a scam?

Not always, because genuine import VAT or duty may be collected by the parcel company. Do not pay through an unexpected link, though. Check the parcel with the courier on contact details you obtained independently. Confirmed counterfeit goods are handled through the Border Force infringement process rather than released because a shopper pays a surprise fee.

How do I report the shop to Nike itself?

Through the contact route on nike.com, opened by typing the address. We print no brand-protection email address, because the ones circulating on third-party sites could not be matched against Nike's own published contacts. Do not expect Nike's ordinary contact channels to authenticate your shoes; keep them as evidence instead.
